steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual picture of a transformer

1. Tokens become vectors  
   • A sentence is split into tokens (words, sub-words, characters, etc.).  
   • Each token is mapped to an embedding vector and receives a “positional encoding” so the model knows where it sits in the sequence.

2. Layers are stacked, and every layer has the same two main blocks  
   Block A: Multi-head self-attention  
     – The model forms three linear projections of every token vector: a query, a key, and a value.  
     – For one “head,” each query is compared (via dot-product) with all keys to obtain attention scores.  
     – The scores are normalized with soft-max, turning them into weights.  
     – The weighted sum of the value vectors is the new, context-aware representation for that token.  
     – Several heads run in parallel, each learning a different notion of “what to pay attention to,” and their results are concatenated and linearly mixed.  

   Block B: Position-wise feed-forward network (FFN)  
     – A small two-layer MLP is applied to every token vector individually, giving the model non-linear capacity beyond the attention operation.

   Residual connections + layer normalization surround each sub-block so information can flow easily and training stays stable.

3. Encoders and decoders play different roles  
   • Encoder (BERT, CLIP, ViT): Stacks only the blocks above. Output is a context-rich embedding for each input token (or an entire sequence).  
   • Decoder (GPT): Adds a third attention module that lets each position attend only to earlier positions (causal masking) so it can generate text autoregressively.  
   • Full encoder–decoder (original “Transformer” for translation): The decoder also has an “encoder-decoder attention” stage that lets it look at the encoder’s outputs while it predicts the next target token.

4. Training and inference  
   • During training, the model compares its predicted token distribution to the known ground-truth tokens (cross-entropy loss); gradients update all parameters.  
   • At inference, a decoder is fed its own previous predictions and keeps generating until an end-of-sequence token or length limit is reached.

5. Why it works  
   • Self-attention gives every token a direct, learned pathway to every other token, capturing long-range patterns without the sequential bottleneck of RNNs.  
   • Multi-head attention lets the model discover multiple kinds of relations (syntax, coreference, topical links) simultaneously.  
   • Stacking layers composes simple relations into higher-level abstractions.  
   • Positional information preserves order even though attention is permutation-invariant by itself.

In short, a transformer repeatedly answers the question “What should each token pay attention to in the rest of the sequence?” then applies lightweight neural processing to the result, building up rich, contextual embeddings that can be used for classification, translation, summarization, text generation, vision tasks, and more.
